messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq is a 34-year-old Lebanese-American man who works as a publisher at a mid-sized independent press in Chicago. He is married, describes his relationship as close, and until approximately eight months ago considered himself someone who moved through the world with confidence. He is now presenting for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 74, reporting severe and pervasive PTSD symptoms following a traumatic event that befell his younger brother.

Eight months ago, Tariq's brother Samir was attacked on a city bus during his evening commute. Samir was beaten severely by two men who had initially appeared simply restless, shifting in their seats and exchanging glances before one produced a blade. Tariq was not present, but he arrived at the hospital within the hour, and what he saw — his brother's face, the sounds Samir made trying to speak, the fragmented account that emerged over days — lodged itself into Tariq's mind in a way that has never resolved into a coherent whole. His memories of that night do not come as a narrative. They arrive in disconnected pieces: the particular fluorescent hum of the hospital corridor, the wet sound of his brother's breathing, a phrase Samir repeated that Tariq still cannot fully hear in his mind without the rest of the memory collapsing. More often, the memories replay not as recollection but as something closer to re-experience — a film, as Tariq describes it, that starts without warning and runs on its own schedule, complete with the auditory texture of sounds he was told about so vividly that they have become his own.

Because the attack happened on a bus, and because the perpetrators were strangers whose menace had been invisible until it was not, Tariq's sense of safety reorganised itself around a single conviction: danger is already present, and the only question is whether he can detect it in time. He now studies the faces and body language of everyone around him with an intensity he cannot suppress, cataloguing micro-expressions and posture shifts for signs of threat. He registers potential weapons — a glass bottle, a belt buckle, a pen left on a conference table — in any room he enters. These habits of vigilance are exhausting, but to Tariq they feel non-negotiable. He avoids unfamiliar places entirely, because in an unknown environment he cannot yet have mapped the exits or assessed the people. This has narrowed his professional life considerably: he has declined two author events in cities he has never visited, offering editorial excuses, and his colleagues have begun to notice his reluctance to attend off-site meetings.

The triggers he encounters are not abstract. Riding public transit — which he once did without thought — now activates the full architecture of his threat system. When Tariq boards a bus, the vigilance ignites immediately: he scans faces, clocks objects, positions himself near the door. And the heightened state of alert does not stay contained to threat monitoring; it pulls the memories forward. The film begins to play. He hears things. The pieces that ordinarily sit disconnected suddenly press toward assembly, and the effort of holding them apart while simultaneously watching the other passengers is overwhelming. He has stopped taking the bus to work and now drives, adding forty minutes to his commute each way. Being naked — the vulnerability of it, the exposure — produces a similar cascade, a bodily sense of defencelessness that opens directly onto the memory fragments and the sounds. Even profound fatigue, which his vigilance guarantees, becomes its own trigger: when he is very tired, his perceptual guard drops, and the memories surface more freely, which in turn reactivates his scanning and his fear, so that exhaustion and hypervigilance feed each other through the night.

The loop has become self-sustaining. The memories themselves, when they arrive, prime his threat system — he emerges from a replay already certain that danger is near, already searching faces, already noticing the glass on the desk. And the threat monitoring, sustained for hours at a time, keeps him in a physiological state in which the memories are never far. His wife has told him, gently and then less gently, that he is not present. What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a night last month when he sat awake until four in the morning, listening to sounds in the apartment, certain something was wrong, and realised he could no longer remember what it had felt like not to be afraid. What he most hopes for, he says quietly, is to be able to hear his brother's voice without hearing everything else alongside it.
